sites.name: Ingalls Creek basin camp, below Longs Pass
sites.capacity: Several established creekside sites plus a small meadow bench east of the crossing; comfortable for two or three parties, more if you spread along the valley
sites.water: Ingalls Creek runs hard and reliably all season. Note there is no water at all between the Esmeralda trailhead and the creek, so the climb over Longs Pass is a dry carry in both directions.
sites.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued wilderness permit from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use; a Northwest Forest Pass or day fee to park. This side of the divide is OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area, so no lottery permit is involved.
sites.notes: The standard base for the Cascadian Couloir and south-side approaches generally, reached from the Esmeralda Basin trailhead over Longs Pass at about 6,200 ft and then dropping roughly 1,400 ft to the valley floor. Access is gated by the Teanaway road: pavement gives way to gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last nine or so miles, rough enough to want patience in a low car and holding snow into early summer. The return sting is real — you finish the day by regaining Longs Pass with an empty water supply. Sites are low and sheltered, so expect mosquitoes through midsummer.

sites.name: Headlight Basin designated sites
sites.capacity: A number of established, signed sites through the basin; the largest legal camping capacity on the Esmeralda side, though it fills on summer weekends with hikers rather than climbers
sites.water: Headlight Creek and snowmelt tarns feed the basin and are dependable through midsummer; by late September the smaller channels can go dry and you may need to hunt for running water
sites.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued trailhead permit for day and overnight use, plus a Northwest Forest Pass to park at Esmeralda. Not part of the Enchantment Permit Area — no lottery, no quota. Camping is prohibited within half a mile of Lake Ingalls itself, which is why the designated sites here exist.
sites.notes: Headlight Basin sits just past Ingalls Pass and is the legal overnight option for parties staging the West Ridge or approaching the north side via Stuart Pass. It buys a comfortable night with the whole south face in view, but it is well short of any route start, so summit day from here is long. Do not be tempted by the shoreline at Lake Ingalls — that closure is enforced and the ground there is fragile. Use the marked pads and skip a fire; open flame is off the table at this elevation. No elevation is recorded for the basin itself because a confident single figure could not be sourced.

sites.name: Upper Ingalls Creek meadows, below Stuart Pass
sites.capacity: A few small parties on durable ground; dispersed rather than developed, with no built sites
sites.water: Headwater streams and snowmelt runnels are usually flowing into late summer, but they thin markedly in a dry year and can require walking downstream to find a reliable source
sites.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness, Cle Elum Ranger District. Free self-issued wilderness permit; Northwest Forest Pass for the Esmeralda trailhead. Outside the Enchantment Permit Area, so no reservation needed — but you are camping on fragile alpine meadow, so pitch on gravel or bare rock rather than vegetation.
sites.notes: Parties climbing the West Ridge often push past Headlight Basin to the meadows at the head of Ingalls Creek so the morning starts near the base of the ridge instead of two hours below it. The ground is a boulder-and-heather mix under the West Wall, and site quality varies a lot within a few hundred yards. From here the West Ridge start is a short climb to the saddle, and Stuart Pass gives access onward toward Goat Pass and the north side. Reports differ on how long snow lingers in these meadows; early-season parties should plan on some of it.

sites.name: Lake Stuart
sites.capacity: Several established sites around the lake, but the real limit is the permit quota — the Stuart Zone releases only a small number of group permits per night
sites.water: The lake and Mountaineer Creek are reliable all season; treat lake water and camp well back from the shore
sites.permit: Enchantment Permit Area, STUART ZONE, Wenatchee River Ranger District. An overnight permit is REQUIRED May 15 through Oct 31, allocated by group through the Recreation.gov advance lottery with a small remainder released otherwise. Outside that window no overnight permit is required, though self-registration at the trailhead is asked for. Day use needs only the free trailhead permit plus a Northwest Forest Pass.
sites.notes: The north-side staging point, used by parties approaching the Complete North Ridge or the Sherpa Glacier from Mountaineer Creek rather than walking around the peak from Ingalls. Road access is seasonal in a way the Teanaway side is not: Forest Road 7601 off Icicle Creek Road generally closes from November until sometime in May, which shortens the window from this side considerably. Where the Stuart Zone boundary falls relative to the upper Mountaineer Creek basin and the Stuart Glacier moraine is genuinely unclear — some maps place Stuart's north side outside the permit zones — so a party bivying high in that basin should confirm with the Wenatchee River Ranger District rather than assume, and carry a permit if in doubt.

sites.name: Goat Pass bivies
sites.capacity: Numerous small rock-and-gravel platforms along the pass; several independent parties can spread out without crowding each other
sites.water: No dependable running water. Snowmelt trickles and lingering patches are usually workable into midsummer, but by late season the pass is dry and you must carry water up or melt snow off the glacier below
sites.permit: Reached from the Esmeralda Basin trailhead over Ingalls Pass and Stuart Pass, so approached on Alpine Lakes Wilderness ground under the Cle Elum Ranger District — free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass to park, no Enchantment lottery permit. The pass sits on the divide, however: a party that continues down into the Mountaineer Creek drainage and camps there is entering the Stuart Zone and needs that overnight permit between May 15 and Oct 31.
sites.notes: The high camp of choice for the upper North Ridge and the Stuart Glacier Couloir when approaching from the Ingalls side, putting the traverse under the glacier and the entry gully within an easy morning. Bivy ground is plentiful and reasonably flat, but the position is exposed and windy, so bring a shelter rather than counting on a sheltered nook. From here the standard line traverses east below the Stuart Glacier above the moraine, with snow crossings well into summer. The water situation is the binding constraint late in the season — treat it as a dry camp unless you have seen recent conditions.

sites.name: North Ridge notch bivy
sites.capacity: Around four or five people at the notch itself, with a scattering of poorer spots higher on the ridge; the good ledges are few and far between once you are on the route
sites.water: None on the ridge. Fill from snowmelt streams on the traverse below the Stuart Glacier before committing, or melt snow from the glacier; there is nothing above.
sites.permit: No separate climbing permit exists for the ridge itself, and the wilderness permit requirement is driven by which drainage you camped in. Parties staging from Ingalls and the Esmeralda side need only the free self-issued Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit; parties who camped in Mountaineer Creek below are in the Stuart Zone and need that overnight permit May 15 to Oct 31. The boundary in the upper basin is not clearly drawn — confirm with the Wenatchee River Ranger District if you intend to bivy low on the north side.
sites.notes: The ridge is gained at roughly 8,200 ft from the upper Stuart Glacier at about 7,800 ft via a snow-filled gully usually climbed on fourth-class rock along its edge, and the notch just above is the last genuinely comfortable bivy before the climbing proper. A second cluster of usable ledges sits several pitches higher, above the junction with the lower west variation, which suits parties splitting the Complete North Ridge over two days. Everything here is an emergency-grade perch rather than a campsite: no water, no shelter, and no easy retreat once committed. Whether to bivy at all is a live disagreement — many parties climb the route in a single push from Goat Pass, and which is better depends on your speed and the descent you have chosen.
